opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think so. It's easy to look back and say, "Oh, fundraising went smoothly, so I should have jumped earlier," but that's a bit of hindsight bias. Investors weren't investing in me as I was two or three years ago. They were investing in me as I am now, with the experience, the track record, and the understanding of the problem I'd built up over that time.

When I was still a student, or just after, I had a lot of ideas, but I didn't really understand what the real pain points were, how systems behave at scale, or what it takes to get people to actually use something you've built. A lot of that came from working on real projects with real users, getting things wrong, and seeing what breaks. If I'd started a company back then, I'd probably have been building something nobody needed, or I'd have built the right thing the wrong way.

There's also timing in the market itself. The window for what we're doing now didn't really exist a few years ago. Demand, infrastructure, and the community's awareness all had to mature. So it's not just about when I was ready, but when the problem was ready to be a business.

So no, I don't really regret it. I think every stage had its value. If anything, the lesson is that when the moment comes and you feel that conviction, you shouldn't hesitate too long. But starting earlier just for the sake of starting earlier, I don't think that would have led to a better outcome.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls the idea that smooth fundraising means he should have started earlier “a bit of hindsight bias.”

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, no, I don't think so. It's tempting to look back and say, well, the money came faster than I expected, so I should have jumped a year earlier. But that's hindsight talking. The reason fundraising felt easy was precisely because of what happened in the years before it. I had spent that time at Tsinghua working on vLLM and on open-source infrastructure, and that work is what people recognized when I walked into those meetings. If I had started earlier, I would have been a different person pitching a weaker story, and the conversations would not have gone the same way.

There's also something about timing that you don't control. In 2023 and early 2024, the attention was all on training, on who could build the biggest model. The understanding that inference would become the real battleground, that serving these models cheaply and reliably is where the engineering problems are, that only became obvious to investors somewhat later. I happened to have been living inside that problem for a while. So the market caught up to what I was doing, rather than me catching up to the market.

And frankly, when I was still a PhD student, I didn't have the conviction yet. I enjoyed the research, I enjoyed being in the open-source community, and I wasn't sure I wanted the responsibility of a company. Starting something before you truly believe in it is a bad idea, no matter how available the capital is. Money being easy to raise is not a reason to start. It's a nice condition, but the reason has to be that you've found a problem you can't stop thinking about and you think you're the right person to solve it.

So if anything, I'd say the lesson isn't "start earlier." It's that the preparation period, even if it looks like a delay from the outside, is often what makes the later speed possible.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the idea that he should have started earlier because fundraising was easier “hindsight talking,” directly identifying the judgment as hindsight bias.

astra-6.text: In hindsight, maybe, but I wouldn’t say that easier fundraising means I should have started earlier. Raising money was one of the uncertainties, but it wasn’t the only one. You also need to feel ready to commit to the problem and build a company around it. So, yes, perhaps I could have taken the leap sooner, but I don’t think fundraising alone is a good reason to regret the timing.

sol-6.1.text: In hindsight, maybe, but I wouldn’t judge the timing just by how easy fundraising was. Before doing it, I thought raising money would be a major obstacle. Once I started, it turned out to be less difficult than I expected. But raising money and building a company are different things. The more important question is whether I was ready and had something worth building. So I might have tested the idea earlier, rather than necessarily starting the company earlier.
